{{Short description|Polish mathematician (1909- 1943)}}
{{distinguish|text=the Moravian composer [[Josef Schreier]], the Austrian mathematician [[Otto Schreier]] or the Polish mathematician [[Juliusz Schauder]]}}

'''Józef Schreier''' ({{IPA|pl|ˈjuzɛf ˈʂrajɛr}}; 18 February 1909, [[Drohobycz]], [[Austria-Hungary]]  – April 1943, Drohobycz, [[Occupied Poland]]) was a [[Polish people|Polish]] [[List of mathematicians|mathematician]] of [[Jewish]] origin, known for his work in [[functional analysis]], [[group theory]] and [[combinatorics]]. He was a member of the [[Lwów School of Mathematics]] and a victim of the [[Holocaust]].

Józef Schreier was born on 18 February 1909 in Drohobycz. His father was a rabbi and doctor of philosophy. His cousin was the musician [[Alfred Schreyer]]. From 1927-31 he studied at the [[University of Lviv|Jan Kazimierz University]] in [[Lwów]].

In his first published paper, he defined what later came to be known as [[Schreier set]]s in order to show that not all [[Banach space]]s possess the weak Banach-Saks property, disproving a conjecture of [[Stefan Banach]] and [[Stanisław Saks]]. Schreier sets were later discovered independently by researchers in [[Ramsey theory]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schreier|first1=J.|title=Ein Gegenbeispiel zur Theorie der schwachen Konvergenz|journal=Studia Mathematica|year=1930|volume=2|issue=1|pages=58–62|doi=10.4064/sm-2-1-58-62|url=https://eudml.org/doc/217264|language=en|issn=0039-3223|doi-access=free|archive-date=2018-03-04|access-date=2018-03-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180304054913/https://eudml.org/doc/217264|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Farmaki|first1=Vassiliki|title=Ramsey and Nash-Williams combinatorics via Schreier families|date=1 May 2004|eprint=math/0404014}}</ref>

Schreier completed his master's degree ''On tournament elimination systems'' in 1932 under the direction of [[Hugo Steinhaus]]. Schreier correctly conjectured that to determine the second largest number in an unordered list requires at least <math>n + \lceil \log_2 n \rceil -2</math> comparisons.<ref>On tournament elimination systems, J. Schreier - Mathesis Polska, 1932</ref> In 1934, he completed his doctorate, ''On finite base in topological groups'' under Banach.<ref>O skończonej bazie w grupach topologicznych</ref>

In 1932 he married Zofia Rosenblatt. Schreier often played [[blindfold chess]].

He was a friend of [[Stanisław Ulam]] and co-authored eight papers with him.<ref>{{cite web|date=1987|title=Publications of Stanislaw M. Ulam|url=https://fas.org/sgp/othergov/doe/lanl/pubs/00326872.pdf|access-date=2020-03-05|website=[[Federation of American Scientists]]|archive-date=2020-08-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200819070535/https://fas.org/sgp/othergov/doe/lanl/pubs/00326872.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> They were the only two undergraduates who attended the meetings at the [[Scottish Café]] in [[Lwów]]. (Schreier contributed ten questions to the [[Scottish Book]].)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Mauldin|first1=R. Daniel|title=The Scottish Book: Mathematics from The Scottish Café, with Selected Problems from The New Scottish Book|date=2015|publisher=Birkhäuser|isbn=9783319228976|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=itYLCwAAQBAJ|language=en}}</ref> Together they proved the [[Baire–Schreier–Ulam theorem]] and [[Schreier–Ulam theorem]].

According to Ulam,
{{Quote
|text=We would meet almost every day, occasionally at the coffee house but more often at my house. His home was in Drohobycz, a little town and petroleum center south of Lwów. What a variety of problems and methods we discussed together! Our work, while still inspired by the methods then current in Lwów, branched into new fields: groups of topological transformations, groups of permutations, pure set theory, general algebra. I believe that some of our papers were among the first to show applications to a wider class of mathematical objects of modern set theoretical methods combined with a more algebraic point of view. We started work on the theory of groupoids, as we called them, or [[semigroups|semi-groups]], as they are called now.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ulam|first1=S. M.|title=Adventures of a Mathematician|date=1991|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=9780520910553|pages=82|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=U2_zEZOHdU4C&pg=PA82|language=en}}</ref>
}}
 
With the outbreak of World War II, Eastern Poland including Drohobycz was occupied by the [[USSR]] in accordance with the [[Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact]]. After [[Operation Barbarossa]], this territory was invaded by [[Nazi Germany]]. The Jews of Drohobycz were confined to the [[Drohobycz Ghetto]]. In April 1943, the Germans discovered—or were informed of—an underground bunker in which Schreier was hiding with other Jews. It took three days for them to force their way in. Schreier committed suicide by [[cyanide]] rather than be captured. Of a prewar Jewish population of 10,000 in Drohobycz, approximately 400 survived the war.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Beery|first1=Janet L.|last2=Greenwald|first2=Sarah J.|last3=Jensen-Vallin|first3=Jacqueline A.|last4=Mast|first4=Maura B.|author4-link=Maura Mast|title=Women in Mathematics: Celebrating the Centennial of the Mathematical Association of America|date=2017|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319666945|pages=71|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eDVBDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA71|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Brief history of the Jews of Drohobycz and Borysław|date=1985|publisher=Drohobycz-Borysław Reunion|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A58tAQAAIAAJ|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Tajemniczy Bruno Schulz|url=http://www.dziennikpolski24.pl/artykul/3093764,tajemniczy-bruno-schulz,id,t.html|work=dziennikpolski24.pl|language=pl|archive-date=2018-03-03|access-date=2018-03-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180303225231/http://www.dziennikpolski24.pl/artykul/3093764,tajemniczy-bruno-schulz,id,t.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Schreier's wife was one of them and later moved to Israel, where she remarried. Schreier's cousin Gina Schreier survived the war in Poland and later emigrated to Brazil with her husband, Bronisław Hoenig. After Ulam’s death, Ulam’s wife passed her the articles they had primarily written together.
